comparison: Both evaluations agree that DN neurons encode multimodal information with strong support. OpenEval cites converging evidence from GLM encoding models, decoding analysis, and temporal dynamics (C22-C24, C62, C4, C19, C23, C83, C53). Peer reviewers describe the data as 'compellingly demonstrate' the central claims about DN cells exhibiting sustained modulation carrying stimulus, response, and outcome information.

Both agree on temporal dynamics findings. OpenEval emphasizes the quantified latency difference with statistical testing (C29: F=10.9, p=0.001) and ramping onset measurements (C8). Peer reviewers accept these as part of the compelling demonstration of DN cells conveying motor and nonmotor variables with temporal dynamics.

Both evaluations support the decoding results. OpenEval highlights systematic logistic regression analysis across time windows and trial-weighting procedures (C30-C36). Peer Reviewer 3 explicitly states the data 'compellingly demonstrate' that DN cells carry information about stimulus, response, and trial outcome, with analyses well-suited to support conclusions.

Disagreement on anatomical tracing conclusions. OpenEval expresses uncertainty due to substantial differences in labeling density between animals (15-25× difference, C39-C44), questioning whether comparable circuits were sampled. Peer reviewers accept the anatomical findings without challenge, with Reviewer 3 affirming the tracer injections demonstrated DN projections to visual attention network targets.

Perfect agreement on temporal dynamics of suppressing/facilitating responses. Both accept the statistical findings (C20-C21) with Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests. Peer reviewers include these as part of analyses well-suited to support conclusions without specific challenges.

Both agree on error-related responses. OpenEval notes the observation is documented (C25) with appropriate speculative interpretation about reward absence (C26). Peer reviewers accept this as part of the broader demonstration that DN cells carry outcome information, explicitly mentioned as compellingly demonstrated.

Disagreement on population comparability. OpenEval questions whether similar encoding fractions (C27) truly indicate comparable populations given vastly different anatomical labeling densities, suggesting possible sampling from different subpopulations. Peer reviewers accept the consistency across animals without raising sampling concerns, supporting generalizability.

Disagreement on functional integration and loop mechanisms. OpenEval finds claims largely speculative (C93-C95 use tentative language) lacking direct evidence for proposed mechanisms despite documented anatomical pathways. Peer reviewers accept the integration framework, with Reviewer 3 stating the study demonstrates DN cells convey variables related to task execution, sequencing, and attention, consistent with the mechanistic framework.

Both agree on compatibility with prior fMRI literature. OpenEval notes appropriate connection to neuroimaging work (C64, C84-C85) with reasonable compatibility given anatomical tracing. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this, with the editor calling it an 'important study' showing cerebellar involvement in cognitive processes at the neuronal level.

Both accept the contextualization within existing literature. OpenEval finds claims appropriately cite supporting literature on expertise, motor planning, FEF function, and ramping as motor preparation signature (C66-C73). Peer reviewers do not challenge these contextual claims, implicitly accepting the background framework.

Both accept cerebellar circuit organization claims. OpenEval notes these are well-supported by cited literature (C75-C80) providing established neuroanatomical context. Peer reviewers do not challenge these literature-based claims, accepting them as framework for interpreting findings.

Both accept theoretical context and prior findings. OpenEval finds claims accurately characterize established theories and appropriately cite supporting literature (C86-C87, C89-C92). Peer reviewers do not challenge these contextual claims about existing theories and related findings.

Both accept background literature claims. OpenEval notes these accurately represent established knowledge and consensus views (C1-C3, C10, C59). Peer reviewers implicitly accept the background framework, with the editor's characterization of this as an important study examining cerebellar cognitive involvement.
OpenEval evaluates methodological and ethical compliance statements (C18, C96-C97) as appropriately documented. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these procedural claims.

Peer reviewers accept anatomical connectivity supporting functional integration (C48-C50, C56, C58, C60), with Reviewer 3 confirming DN projections to visual attention network. OpenEval addresses overlapping claims in R5 and R9 but not this specific grouping.

Peer reviewers express uncertainty about causal role of DN in the task (C11, C60, C74, C88). While editor and Reviewer 3 find evidence convincing, Reviewer 2 explicitly states the manuscript doesn't address whether this brain region is relevant to the task, suggesting need for inactivation experiments. OpenEval addresses these claims in R1 and R9 but not as a distinct causal mechanism grouping.
